report:
(Fictional case study for training. Not a real investigation.)

Investigation summary

What happened

At 02:47:12 on 12/08/2026 (times in this report are local time, UTC+8), an empty 220 t class rigid haul truck, HT-407, descending the main ramp of the Stage 4 open pit at Bindarra Gold Mine at 37 km/h struck the right side of light vehicle LV-118 at 24 km/h as LV-118 came out of the RL 312 dewatering spur. LV-118 rolled onto its left side against the inner windrow.

The sole occupant, a grade control technician employed by a survey subcontractor, Hallorn Survey & Geotechnical, was on the third night shift at the mine and sustained a fractured left clavicle, three fractured left ribs and a small pneumothorax. The technician was extricated at 03:14, 27 minutes after the collision, and was flown to the metropolitan trauma centre at 07:40. LV-118 was destroyed and HT-407 returned to service on 14/08/2026. The Stage 4 pit stood down for 9 hours 15 minutes, the main ramp below RL 340 was closed for 22 hours, and the occurrence was notified to the State Mines Inspectorate as a reportable injury.

What the investigation found

Works order WO-26-4471 opened the spur as routine earthworks, so no management of change record was raised. It is very likely that this contributed to what followed, because the traffic management plan owner, the survey department and the contractor's technical services group were never told of the new intersection. The guideline under which the plan is made defined neither a significant change nor a basis for choosing positive-call intersections, and it probably contributed by making inaction the default.

The spur had 41 m of sight distance against a 96 m stopping distance, which very likely contributed to neither driver becoming aware of the other in time. The absence of a stop control or warning sign probably contributed to the light vehicle leaving the spur without stopping, as did the issue of the driver's access card without a check for the pit driving assessment. The plan required a positive call only at nine listed intersections and the spur was not one, so neither driver called, which probably contributed to the convergence. The S4-LOAD geofence suppressed the collision awareness system at the spur without the operators being told, which probably contributed through the expectation that a quiet system meant an empty ramp, although that effect cannot be measured. It is extremely likely that neither driver was aware of the other until the truck came over the crest, and the impact followed within about six seconds.

Airborne dust was recorded as likely to have existed and about as likely as not to have influenced the sighting, and it was not carried into the contributing factors. The extrication arrangement and the 14 night haul roster did not contribute to the collision. Whether the haul truck operator was fatigued could not be determined.

The truck operator's 1.4 second response and steering right reduced the impact speed from 37 km/h to 24 km/h, and the intact roll-over protection structure and the fastened seatbelt also limited the outcome. [NOT ESTABLISHED: the light vehicle driver's own interview is not among the finalised interviews, so the driver's account is available only as reflected in the evidence descriptions and the investigator's notes]

What has been done as a result

The RL 312 spur was closed on the night, and the Mining Manager directed at 05:10 that a positive call be made before entering any Stage 4 intersection. Survey measured ten other unlisted roads on 14/08/2026 and closed two below the sight distance minimum pending a stop control. Recommendations on the works order exclusion, the plan and the geofences remain open.

Safety message

A road added to an operating pit by a works order can bypass every check that would have put it on the map, the call list and the alert system. Operators and crews should treat any new junction on a haul road as an intersection until it has been surveyed and controlled, and should call before entering it.

The occurrence

Before the shift

Bore DW-14 was energised and the RL 312 dewatering spur was first used by light vehicles on 02/08/2026. Works order WO-26-4471 had been raised on 28/07/2026 for 240 m of access road to the bore, and the works log recorded the earthworks complete on 31/07/2026. The "ROAD CLOSED - CONSTRUCTION" sign that had stood at the spur mouth during construction was removed on 02/08/2026, and nothing was installed in its place. No warning sign, give-way control or delineation was added at any point before the collision.

At about 22:10 on 04/08/2026, a dewatering technician came out of the spur onto the main ramp with a descending haul truck about 60 m up the ramp. The technician reversed back into the spur and let the truck pass. The technician submitted hazard report HAZ-2026-0917 at 23:48 the same night and wrote:

  • "The problem is you cannot see up the ramp from that road. There is a rise in the ramp and a windrow along the side and you are out on the road before you can see anything." [Hazard report HAZ-2026-0917]
  • "The trucks are doing forty coming down empty. I do not think they know the road is there." [Hazard report HAZ-2026-0917]

The Dewatering Superintendent closed the report on 06/08/2026 with this entry: "Spoke with the dewatering crew at pre-start 05/08 and reminded them to take care entering the main ramp and to give way to haul trucks at all times. Crew acknowledged. Trucks have right of way on the ramp per the traffic management plan. No further action required. Closed." The risk rating was reduced from Medium to Low on closure, and the report was not referred to the mining department, the contractor, the survey department or the traffic management plan owner.

On 09/08/2026 the Bindarra gatehouse issued a site access card to the light vehicle driver, a grade control technician employed by a survey subcontractor, after a 20 minute briefing on muster points, speed limits and personal protective equipment. The gatehouse held no record of the Bindarra site-specific supplement or the light vehicle pit driving assessment, and did not ask for either. The driver's first of three night shifts at Bindarra began that evening.

The night shift and approach

Dispatch called the Stage 4 pit back to work after crib at 02:22:41. The pit channel was logged continuously, and the investigator listened to the whole period. HT-407 called at the RL 360 crossover going up at 02:28:10 and at the ROM pad turn-off at 02:37:20, and each call was acknowledged. At 02:46:21 it called at the RL 360 crossover going down, and dispatch acknowledged that call at 02:46:24. Neither vehicle made any transmission about the RL 312 spur, the dewatering bore or a light vehicle being in the pit. LV-118 made no transmission that shift beyond logging on at 18:04 at the start of shift.

The light vehicle driver finished a set of levels at the DW-14 collar and drove the 240 m spur towards the main ramp. The timing of this movement is estimated, from about 02:45 to about 02:47, and rests on the driver's account and the 240 m length of the spur. The driver later gave the time as "about ten to three", which is later than the recorded collision, so that time was not used. LV-118 was not dispatched and carried only a passive collision awareness tag, so its movements before the spur mouth are known only from that account and the scene evidence. The night shift supervisor did not know a light vehicle was in the pit, and no permit, call-in or board existed by which the supervisor could have known.

HT-407 was descending the main ramp empty at 37 km/h. The haul truck operator was on night 10 of a 14 night swing and described the night as ordinary. The in-cab road network, last published on 24/07/2026, showed the main ramp with no intersection at RL 312.

At 02:47:06.0 the fleet management system recorded the truck's last steady data point, at 37 km/h and 53 m above the spur mouth. The survey places the first sight of the light vehicle's beacon over the crest at that distance. At 02:47:07.4, with the truck 38.5 m above the mouth, service brake pressure rose from 0 to 620 kPa in 0.4 seconds, the retarder went to maximum and 14 degrees of right steering was applied. The download gave a 1.4 second response. The operator estimated the light vehicle was about 40 m away when first seen, and the survey figure of 53 m is the measured distance.

At 02:47:09.2 the collision awareness system logged a proximity event at 21.4 m with a closing speed of 32 km/h. The alert was suppressed by the S4-LOAD geofence, so nothing was presented in the cab.

The collision

The impact occurred at 02:47:12.0, at 24 km/h, 6.2 m into the ramp from the spur mouth and 3.1 m out from the toe of the inner windrow. The truck's accelerometer logged 1.9 g longitudinal. The light vehicle was turning right out of the spur to go up the ramp, so its right side faced the descending truck. The front left of HT-407 struck the right side of LV-118.

The truck's braked tyre scuff began 38.5 m up-ramp of the spur mouth and ran 58 m to its resting position, deviating 1.4 m to the right over its first 20 m. A continuous gouge ran 18.4 m down-ramp from the impact position and changed from tyre scuff to body panel gouge at 11.2 m, where LV-118 went over. It came to rest on its left side against the inner windrow, facing down-ramp. Right-side glass and mirror fragments lay from 4.8 m to 14 m down-ramp of the impact position. The roll-over protection structure was deformed inward at the right rear mounting and was not breached. The driver's seatbelt was fastened and its webbing carried loading marks. The 4.5 m beacon whip was sheared at its base and recovered 9 m from the vehicle, and its lamp worked when tested. Damage to HT-407 was confined to the front left bumper, the left mudguard and the lower two steps of the access ladder. The truck stopped about 19 m below the intersection, at about 02:47:19.

The light vehicle driver was conscious throughout. The driver sustained a fractured left clavicle, three fractured left ribs and a small pneumothorax. The door on the resting side was against the ground.

The response

The haul truck operator made the first call at 02:47:41: "I've hit a light vehicle on the ramp at three-twelve." Dispatch stopped all Stage 4 traffic at 02:48:01 and told the operator to stay in the cab until the traffic was stopped. At 02:48:44 dispatch told the operator the ramp was clear above and below the truck, and the operator then went to the light vehicle. At 02:49:30 the operator reported that the driver was conscious and talking but could not get out because the door was against the ground. The supervisor told the operator not to move the driver and to wait for the emergency response team. The supervisor was at the ROM pad and arrived about five minutes later.

Dispatch paged the emergency response team at 02:48. The first response vehicle entered the pit at 02:51 and reached the scene at 02:54. The second responder, called from the accommodation village 11 km from the gatehouse, arrived with the hydraulic rescue tool at 03:07. The driver was extricated through the rear of the vehicle at 03:14, 27 minutes after the collision, and reached the surface medical facility at 03:41. The driver was flown to the metropolitan trauma centre at 07:40. The post-incident review found the extrication was delayed by approximately 9 minutes, measured from 02:58 to the second responder's arrival, and recorded that the delay did not affect the clinical outcome on this occasion. The response arrangements remain under examination.

Immediate actions recorded in notification ORR-OCC-2026-0332 were that the Stage 4 pit was stood down, the main ramp was closed below RL 340 and the spur was barricaded and closed to all traffic. Both vehicles were isolated and left in position, and the scene was photographed and surveyed before recovery. The haul truck operator and the shift supervisor were stood down for the rest of the shift, and both tested negative for drugs and alcohol. The Mining Manager issued a site-wide direction at 05:10 requiring a positive call on the pit channel before entering any intersection in the Stage 4 pit, listed in the plan or not, until further notice. The contractor's technical services group downloaded the fleet management and collision awareness data from HT-407 at 09:30 and provided it to the investigation unopened.

Context

This section describes the site, the organisations and people involved, the vehicles, the rules that applied and the systems fitted.

Site and pit

Bindarra Gold Mine operated the Stage 4 open pit, which was served by a main ramp running approximately north-west on a 9.1 per cent descending grade. The ramp was 24 m wide between windrows and traffic kept left, so a descending truck ran on the open, pit side of the road and an ascending vehicle ran on the wall side. The surface was dry and well maintained when examined at 06:20 on 12/08/2026.

The RL 312 dewatering spur joined the ramp on a descending truck's left, on the inside of a left-hand bend, at an included angle of 71 degrees. The spur mouth was 34 m below a convex grade break in the ramp, where the descent steepened and which the crews called the crest. The spur was a 240 m access road to dewatering bore DW-14, cut under works order WO-26-4471, completed on 31/07/2026 and first used by light vehicles on 02/08/2026.

There was no fixed lighting anywhere in the Stage 4 pit. The only lighting was vehicle lighting and the light plants at the loading face, 1.1 km away and out of sight behind the crest. Moonset was at 23:18 on the previous evening, and the collision at 02:47 was in darkness.

Organisations

Orrabinda Resources was the mine operator, and its Mining Manager owned the traffic management plan BIN-TMP-004. Tarrowen Mining Services was the haul contractor, and its technical services group configured the collision awareness system. Hallorn Survey & Geotechnical was the survey subcontractor that employed the light vehicle driver, and it had held a recognition agreement with Orrabinda Resources since 2023.

People

The haul truck operator drove HT-407 on the Stage 4 night shift. The operator had 14 months at Bindarra, 4 years 2 months with Tarrowen, 7 years on 220 t class rigid haul trucks and 11 years in open pit mining. The operator's verification of competency on type was issued in 06/2025 and the annual refresher was completed in 02/2026. At the time of the collision the operator was on night 10 of a 14 night swing, 8 hours 47 minutes into a 12 hour 30 minute shift, after 6 hours 30 minutes of sleep in the preceding day.

The light vehicle driver was a grade control technician employed by Hallorn Survey & Geotechnical. The driver completed the Hallorn general mining induction, a two hour online module, on 24/07/2026. The driver worked three night shifts at Bindarra, on 09/08, 10/08 and 11/08, and the collision occurred on the third.

The night shift supervisor had 19 years in open pit mining, 8 years with Tarrowen and 2 years 6 months in the supervisory role. The supervisor was responsible for the haul fleet, the excavators, the ancillary fleet, the dozers and the dispatch operator, and was not responsible for the dewatering crew, the survey contractor or any other light vehicle in the pit. The supervisor was on night 10 of 14, the same pattern as the crews supervised.

Vehicles

HT-407 was a 220 t class rigid haul truck, commissioned in 03/2021, with 31,480 engine hours. Its last 500 hour service was on 28/07/2026 with no defects carried. The monthly brake performance test on 03/08/2026 gave a mean deceleration of 0.80 m/s2 net in the empty condition on a 9 per cent descending grade, and a test on 14/08/2026 before the unit returned to service gave 0.82 m/s2 net.

LV-118 was a 4WD utility in service since 02/2024, with 61,200 km, and its last periodic service was on 17/07/2026. It was fitted with a certified roll-over protection structure, a 4.5 m amber beacon whip, reflective marking to the site standard and a UHF radio. It was not dispatched, carried no fleet management system and had a passive collision awareness system tag.

Regulatory framework

Mines Safety Guideline MSG-14 revision 4, issued by the State Mines Inspectorate in 2021, was made under regulation 6.22 of the Mining Operations Safety Regulations 2018. Compliance with the guideline is one way of discharging the regulation, which requires only that "the operator shall manage the risks arising from the interaction of vehicles at the mine".

Clause 3.2 of the guideline requires the traffic management plan to be reviewed at intervals not exceeding twelve months, and following any significant change to the mine's road network, vehicle fleet or operating pattern. Clause 3.5 provides that the plan is a site document, not approved by the Inspectorate and not required to be submitted to it except on request following an occurrence or an inspection. Clause 5.1 requires the operator to nominate the intersections, crossings and other interaction zones at which positive communication is required before entry, and to record them in the plan. Clause 5.4 requires a light vehicle to be detectable by a heavy vehicle operator, and allows this to be provided by line of sight, elevated marking, radio communication, a proximity detection system, or a combination of these. The guideline does not define "significant change", sets no minimum number of interaction zones and gives no basis for nominating them.

Bindarra rules

BIN-TMP-004 revision 7 was issued on 12/11/2025, with its next review due on 12/11/2026. Clause 4.1 requires light vehicles to "give way to heavy vehicles at all times and in all circumstances". Clause 4.3.1 requires a positive call on the relevant pit channel before entering any intersection listed at Appendix B, and entry is not to be made until the call is acknowledged or the channel is confirmed clear. Clause 4.3.2 provides that at intersections not listed, vehicles give way under clause 4.1 and no call is required. Appendix B lists nine intersections, and the RL 312 spur was not one of them. A laminated board in each crib room reproduced Appendix B, and the Stage 4 board was the 12/11/2025 issue.

Clause 6.2 requires the available sight distance at every intersection to be not less than the stopping distance of the largest vehicle using the road at the posted speed, and in no case less than 120 m. Where that cannot be achieved, the intersection is to be controlled by a stop control, signalised control or traffic controller. Clause 6.4 requires every intersection shown on the road layout drawing at Schedule 1 to have an intersection warning sign 50 m in advance on each approach, a give-way control on the minor road and delineation at the mouth. Clause 9.1 requires the plan to be reviewed annually and after any significant change to the mine's road network. Schedule 1 was dated 12/11/2025 and the RL 312 spur did not appear on it.

Orrabinda's Management of Change procedure ORR-PRO-022 requires, at clause 5.2, a management of change record before a change to the mine's road network. Clause 5.3 excludes routine earthworks carried out under a works order within an approved pit design where no new plant or vehicle type is introduced. Clause 5.4 provides that where a record is raised, the impact assessment includes referral to the traffic management plan owner, the survey department for the fleet management system road network, and the contractor's technical services group for the collision awareness system configuration.

Orrabinda's Contractor Management Standard ORR-STD-009 allows, at clause 7.3, a contractor's own general induction to be accepted as equivalent to the Bindarra general induction where the contractor holds a current recognition agreement. Clause 7.4 provides that this equivalence does not extend to the Bindarra site-specific supplement or the Bindarra light vehicle pit driving assessment, which are to be completed at site by every person who will drive in an operating pit. Clause 7.5 makes the engaging department responsible for verifying this before a site access card is issued.

Systems

The fleet management system in-cab road network for the Stage 4 pit was last published on 24/07/2026 and did not contain the RL 312 spur.

The collision awareness system on the Stage 4 haul fleet operated at Level 8, operator advisory. Level 9 automated intervention was available on the fleet and was not enabled at Bindarra. An advisory alert was raised when a vehicle tag entered the 60 m detection ring at a closing rate above 10 km/h, except inside a suppression geofence, where no alert was raised at any range and a proximity event was logged only once the range fell below 25 m. The S4-LOAD geofence was drawn on 14/03/2025 around the Stage 4 loading face to stop nuisance alerts, and was extended northward on 09/06/2026 when the loading face advanced. The extension carried the boundary up the main ramp for the first time, to a point 180 m up-ramp of the RL 312 intersection. [NOT ESTABLISHED: the size of the 09/06/2026 S4-LOAD extension, because the configuration gives only the new boundary]

Emergency response arrangements

The night shift was rostered with one qualified mines rescue paramedic, based at the surface medical facility. A second responder, who must be present before any extrication is begun, was called in from the accommodation village 11 km from the gatehouse. That responder travelled in the second response vehicle, which was garaged at the village and carried the hydraulic rescue tool. The effect of this arrangement on the extrication is still being examined.

Matters not established

[NOT ESTABLISHED: whether Hallorn Survey & Geotechnical issued the Bindarra site supplement to the light vehicle driver, because Hallorn's records for it are outstanding]

[NOT ESTABLISHED: whether Tarrowen supervisors were ever trained on BIN-TMP-004, because no training record was found]

[NOT ESTABLISHED: whether the technical services group told anyone at Orrabinda Resources or Tarrowen of the June 2026 geofence extension, because this is not known]

Safety analysis

This analysis follows the conditions that built an unlisted, unsigned intersection with a short sight line into a haul road, then the controls that did not apply there, then the actions of the two drivers and the collision itself. It closes with the factors that reduced severity and the matters considered and not found contributing.

The intersection that was not an intersection

The external guideline left the mine wide discretion. Clause 3.2 of MSG-14 requires the traffic management plan to be reviewed within twelve months and after any significant change to the road network, and clause 5.1 requires the operator to nominate the intersections at which positive communication is required. The guideline states that it "does not define 'significant change' at 3.2, and contains no example of one. It does not say who nominates the interaction zones at 5.1 or on what basis, and sets no minimum." Bindarra's plan met the guideline on its face, because it had been reviewed within twelve months and nominated nine interaction zones, so the mine was not in breach. The guideline probably contributed, because a defined trigger would have required the plan to be reopened when a road was added, and a stated basis for nomination would have given an intersection failing the sight distance rule a claim on the list. However, the mine could have held an out-of-cycle review under its own clause 9.1 at any time and could have listed every intersection it had, and nothing inside the mine put the question to the plan's owner. That evidence limited the guideline's effect to making inaction the default, which is why its contribution is held at likely and no higher.

Inside the mine, the procedure for managing change had a gap that the works order passed through. ORR-PRO-022 clause 5.2 requires a management of change record before "a change to the mine's road network", but clause 5.3 states that this "does not apply to routine earthworks carried out under a works order within an approved pit design, where no new plant or vehicle type is introduced." WO-26-4471, raised on 28/07/2026, cut 240 m of access to bore DW-14, classified the work as routine earthworks and recorded that management of change was not required. Its handover field read "N/A". The three referrals that clause 5.4 attaches to a management of change record are to the traffic management plan owner, the survey department for the in-cab road network and the contractor's technical services group for the collision awareness system geofences. None was made, because the works order form has no fields for them. Of the fourteen new Stage 4 roads cut since the review of 12/11/2025, the three raised under a management of change record were all referred to the plan's owner, and none of the eleven raised under a works order was. It is very likely that opening the spur under a works order contributed to the conditions that followed. A referral is not itself a control, and no out-of-cycle review had been held in the plan's eleven years, so the plan's owner might have left the spur to the annual review. That possibility accounts for the term not being higher.

The consequences were direct. The in-cab road network last published on 24/07/2026 showed the main ramp with no intersection at RL 312. The spur joined the ramp inside the S4-LOAD suppression geofence. The spur appeared on neither Schedule 1 nor Appendix B of the plan, and it had no sign or control of any kind.

The sight line and the warnings that preceded the collision

The survey of 13/08/2026 placed the spur mouth 34 m below a convex grade break. A truck operator at an eye height of 5.80 m first had line of sight to the spur mouth at 41 m and to the top of the light vehicle's 4.5 m beacon whip at 53 m. A driver at the mouth, at an eye height of 1.45 m, first had line of sight to a descending truck at 38 m, and the 1.6 m inner windrow hid the truck's lower body before that. The stopping distance of the truck empty at the posted 40 km/h on the 9 per cent descent was 96 m, and about 68 m on brakes alone from 37 km/h at the recorded 0.78 m/s2. Clause 6.2 of BIN-TMP-004 requires available sight distance of not less than the stopping distance and in no case less than 120 m. The intersection met neither limb. With twice the sight line, the same 1.4 second response and the same braking would have stopped the truck short of the spur. The sight line very likely contributed to neither driver becoming aware of the other in time. A sight line is only hazardous once something is in it, and the other conditions in this analysis put the two vehicles there.

The geometry had been described in writing seven days earlier. A dewatering technician came out of the spur on 04/08/2026 in front of a truck about 60 m away, reversed back into the spur and submitted hazard report HAZ-2026-0917 that night. The report named the rise, the windrow, the missing sign and the missing give-way. The prompt report worked as intended, but it was closed two days later with a reminder to the crew, with the risk rating reduced from Medium to Low, and with no referral to the mining department, the survey department or the plan's owner. The search of the reporting system found three other reports, from 03/2025, 09/2025 and 02/2026, each describing a light vehicle and a haul truck meeting unexpectedly at an unlisted intersection. All were closed within three days with a reminder to the crew, and none led to a change to Appendix B, to Schedule 1 or to any physical control.

Controls that did not apply at the spur

Clause 6.2 also requires that, where the sight distance cannot be achieved, the intersection be controlled by a stop control, signalised control or traffic controller. The survey gave 41 m against a stopping distance of 96 m, so that requirement applied to the spur. Clause 6.4, which requires a warning sign 50 m in advance, a give-way control and delineation, applies only to intersections on the Schedule 1 drawing, and the spur was not on it. The spur therefore had no warning sign on either approach, no stop or give-way control, no delineation and no posted speed, and the construction sign at the mouth had been removed on 02/08/2026 with nothing put in its place. The absence of a stop control and warning sign probably contributed to the light vehicle leaving the spur without stopping. A stop at the mouth would have held the light vehicle there while the truck was within its 38 m of view, as the technician's reversal showed on 04/08. Against that, 38 m is about four seconds of a truck at 37 km/h, a thin margin even from a standstill, and the effect of a sign on the truck's speed rests on the operator's own view that they would have been at twenty. Those limits keep the term at likely.

The call requirement was written so that it could not apply at the spur. Clause 4.3.1 requires a positive call before entering an intersection listed at Appendix B, and clause 4.3.2 states that at other intersections "No call is required." Appendix B lists nine intersections, and its note provides that an intersection is added only where it appears on the Schedule 1 drawing and the annual review assesses it as needing positive communication. Nothing in the plan allows an addition between reviews. The pit channel recording shows the practice working as written, because HT-407 called and was acknowledged at the RL 360 crossover at 02:28 going up, at the ROM pad turn-off at 02:37 and at the RL 360 crossover at 02:46:21 coming down, 51 seconds before the collision. It made no call at the spur. The haul truck operator and the night shift supervisor each described the same practice, that calls are made at the intersections on the crib room board and nowhere else. The light vehicle driver's interview is not finalised, so the only material from the driver is the driver's corrected account of the approach. It is very likely that the limit of the call requirement to listed intersections contributed to neither driver making a call. LV-118 made no transmission at all that shift beyond logging on at 18:04 at the start of shift. A call from either vehicle would have been heard by the other, by dispatch and by the supervisor, so the absence of a call very likely contributed to neither driver being aware of the other. A call gives knowledge rather than separation, and the two vehicles would still have had to resolve who went first over 41 m of sight line.

The collision awareness system was fitted and working, but not where it was needed. It operated at Level 8, advisory only. The S4-LOAD geofence, drawn on 14/03/2025 to stop nuisance alerts at the loading face, was extended northward on 09/06/2026 as a configuration task by the contractor's technical services group, and carried the boundary up the main ramp to 180 m up-ramp of the later spur intersection. The extension was not recorded in the traffic management plan or reviewed against it. The log recorded a proximity event at 02:47:09.2 at 21.4 m and 32 km/h closing, with the alert suppressed. In the twelve months to 11/08/2026, HT-407 raised 1,684 advisory alerts, every one outside the geofence. Across the fleet, 68 proximity events inside it were suppressed, nine of them a light vehicle on the main ramp below the boundary, all after 09/06/2026. No training record on site covers the geofences. The night shift supervisor said they had known the system was off at the dig since about the middle of 2025 and had not known the geofence had been extended to the ramp.

The haul truck operator said in interview that they had never had the system sound below the crest in fourteen months and that they "assumed there was nothing to go off at", and the operator did not know it was suppressed there. The operator's own protected safety report, which is described here by role and not quoted, gave the same understanding. The system probably contributed to neither driver being aware of the other, through the expectation that a quiet system meant an empty ramp, although that effect cannot be measured. The timing evidence points the other way. An unsuppressed alert would have sounded at about 02:47:06.5, half a second after the beacon came into view and about a second before the brakes went on. The system is advisory and the operator was descending at the speed every operator uses on that ramp, and the operator's own remedy was a sign and not the system. The term is therefore held at likely, at the standard of proof and no higher.

The access card process left the light vehicle driver without the training that the standard required. ORR-STD-009 clause 7.4 states that a contractor's induction equivalence "does not extend to the Bindarra site-specific supplement, or to the Bindarra light vehicle pit driving assessment, which shall be completed at site by every person who will drive a vehicle in an operating pit and shall not be substituted." Clause 7.5 makes the engaging department responsible for verifying this before a card is issued. The gatehouse issued the card on 09/08/2026 against Hallorn's recognition agreement after a 20 minute briefing, and held no record of either item and was not asked for one. The driver's training file shows no pit driving assessment and the driver had never seen BIN-TMP-004. The assessment is where a driver learns to approach a mouth that cannot be seen out of by stopping and looking again, and it probably contributed to the light vehicle leaving the spur without stopping. The driver told the investigation they would have called if told to call. However, the driver was already applying the rule the assessment teaches first, to give way to heavy vehicles, and the plan requires no call at an unlisted intersection, so the assessment would not have taught the driver to call at RL 312. Whether the site supplement was issued could not be determined, because the Hallorn records for it were not available. No copy of the assessment's content is held, and that and the driver's existing practice keep the term at likely.

The convergence and the light vehicle's movement

HT-407 was descending empty at 37 km/h with no intersection on its in-cab map, no sign, no call and no alert. LV-118 was coming out of the spur towards a mouth with 38 m of sight line and no control, with no call and no knowledge of the truck. The first sighting available to the truck operator was the beacon at 53 m, six seconds before impact. No radio log, download, collision awareness log or interview showed that either driver knew of the other before then. The night shift supervisor did not know a light vehicle was in the pit, and said there is no permit, call-in or board by which they could have. It is extremely likely that neither driver was aware of the other until the truck came over the crest. Nothing in the six seconds that remained could have prevented the collision. The light vehicle's movements before the spur mouth rest on the driver's account alone, so [NOT ESTABLISHED: the light vehicle's movements before the spur mouth other than the driver's own account].

The driver's account, corrected by the driver on read-back from stopped to slowed, was that the driver slowed at the mouth, looked right up the ramp, saw nothing and drove out at about 25 km/h, and did not believe they had come to a complete stop. The collision awareness log placed the light vehicle at the mouth at 02:47:09.2 with the truck 21.4 m above, and the impact was 2.8 seconds later. The truck was within the driver's 38 m of view from about 02:47:07.4, nearly two seconds before the driver reached the mouth, so the driver's look came when the truck was beyond what their position allowed them to see. Clause 4.1 requires light vehicles to give way to heavy vehicles at all times, which is the rule the driver described applying. Without the light vehicle on the ramp there is no collision, and it is extremely likely that the light vehicle driving out of the spur without stopping contributed to the collision. A stop at the mouth would very likely have shown the driver the truck, as it did for the technician on 04/08, although a stop is only as good as the look from it at 38 m.

Impact and injury

The truck's front left struck the right side of the light vehicle at 02:47:12.0 at 24 km/h, 6.2 m into the ramp from the spur mouth, and the accelerometer logged 1.9 g longitudinal. The light vehicle was turning right to go up the ramp, with its right side towards the truck. It was pushed 18.4 m down the ramp and rolled onto its left side against the inner windrow at about 11.2 m, and the evidence is conclusive on both points because the recorded data, the damage and the debris agree. The roll-over protection structure was deformed inward at the right rear mounting and was not breached, and the seatbelt was fastened with loading marks on the webbing. The driver sustained a fractured left clavicle, three fractured left ribs and a small pneumothorax, and was conscious throughout. The structure and the restraint held, and the injuries were those of a side impact and roll-over in those conditions.

What reduced the severity

The truck operator's response limited the impact. The download recorded the last steady data point at 02:47:06.0 at 37 km/h, 53 m above the spur mouth, and brake pressure rising from 0 to 620 kPa from 02:47:07.4 with the retarder at maximum and 14 degrees of right steering. That is a 1.4 second response, inside the 1.5 seconds that the plan's stopping distance calculation allows. Mean deceleration of 0.78 m/s2 net compared with the unit's tested 0.80. Impact speed was 24 km/h and would have been 37 km/h without braking, which removed about 58 per cent of the impact energy. The scuff deviated 1.4 m to the right over its first 20 m, away from the open side where the drop was more than 100 m, and the light vehicle came to rest against the inner windrow and not over the edge. It is very likely that the operator's braking and steering reduced the severity of the outcome.

Matters considered and not found contributing

A wet or slippery ramp was considered and was very unlikely. The met station recorded no precipitation and the last rainfall was 26 days earlier. The water cart's last pass was at 01:10 and the investigator found the ramp dry at 06:20. The braked scuff ran continuously for 58 m with no sign of a locked wheel, and the deceleration achieved was the figure the truck achieves dry.

Reduced brake performance was considered and was very unlikely. The monthly test on 03/08/2026 gave 0.80 m/s2 net and the test on 14/08/2026 gave 0.82. The download gave 0.78, which is inside the scatter of the two tests. No brake, retarder or park brake defect had been raised in the previous twelve months, and the pre-start sheet for 11/08/2026 recorded no defects.

The effect of airborne dust on the ramp is a matter still being examined, its existence being likely and its influence about as likely as not. The water cart pass was 7 minutes overdue against the 90 minute instruction. The dust monitor on the RL 328 bench, 180 m up-ramp and above the grade break, logged PM10 at 142 micrograms per cubic metre in the ten minutes covering the occurrence against a shift mean of 88. The truck operator said some dust was hanging around, that the cart had been through earlier and that they could not say it made a difference. Against that, 142 is well below the site trigger of 250 and measures particulate at the monitor head and not what could be seen from either cab. The light vehicle driver said the air was clear, although that was a description of the spur below the windrow and not of the ramp above the crest. The beacon was sighted at 53 m, the first point at which the survey says it could be seen at all, and the response from there was 1.4 seconds. That leaves little room for a dust delay to hide in, although the sighting is inferred from the last steady data point and the survey and not recorded, so a fraction of a second at the edge of the lights cannot be excluded. [NOT ESTABLISHED: any measurement of visibility from either cab]. Nothing is carried from this matter into the findings.

Fatigue of the haul truck operator could not be settled. The operator was on night 10 of 14, 8 hours 47 minutes into a 12 hour 30 minute shift, at 02:47 and inside the window of lowest circadian alertness. The operator's voluntary sleep record gave between 5 and 7 hours on each of the preceding days, 6 hours 30 minutes on the last. The operator said they were tired "the way you are on night ten", and detecting a hazard in an unlit pit is a task that fatigue degrades first. However, the operator also said "Not falling asleep tired ... I was awake and I was driving properly", every limit in the contractor's fatigue standard was met, and the recorded response of 1.4 seconds inside the plan's 1.5 seconds and the immediate braking and steering showed none of the usual signs. The evidence is evenly balanced as to whether the operator was fatigued to a degree that degraded performance, and a detailed fatigue assessment would be needed to settle it. That assessment was not pursued, because even if fatigue were present it would not have changed the outcome. Braking at 0.78 m/s2 from 53 m, a response time of zero would still have ended in a collision, at about 17 km/h and not 24 km/h.

The roster as an organisational factor was tested separately. It is virtually certain that the Stage 4 haul roster of 14 nights on and 7 off existed, and that every limit in the fatigue standard was met, including 14 consecutive night shifts and a 10 hour break. Its influence on this occurrence is unlikely, because the one mechanism it could have worked through, a slow response, is contradicted by the recorded data. The roster is nevertheless a standing exposure at the importance of likely, because it puts every haul operator at the wheel in the small hours of a tenth, twelfth and fourteenth consecutive night, where the defence against an unlit hazard at an unlisted intersection is the operator's own detection and response. It is therefore in the group of other factors that increased risk, and not among the contributing factors.

Other factors that increased risk

The night shift extrication arrangement is a matter still being examined, its existence being virtually certain, its influence on this occurrence unlikely and its importance very likely. The night shift is rostered with one qualified mines rescue paramedic at the surface medical facility. The second responder, who must be present before any extrication, comes from the accommodation village 11 km from the gatehouse in the vehicle that carries the hydraulic rescue tool. Dispatch paged the team at 02:48, the first response vehicle reached the scene at 02:54, the paramedic's primary survey was complete and the extrication plan made at 02:58, the second responder arrived at 03:07, and the driver was extricated at 03:14. The post-incident review measured the delay at approximately 9 minutes and found it did not affect the clinical outcome, because the injuries were stable and the driver was conscious throughout. The collision and its injuries were complete before the team was paged, so the arrangement did not influence this occurrence. It remains a standing gap because nothing in it changes with the severity of the casualty.

Supervision of light vehicles in the pit

The night shift supervisor told the investigation that they did not know a light vehicle was in the Stage 4 pit that night. The supervisor said there is no permit, radio call-in, board or check at the pit entry, and that anyone with a site access card can drive in. This is the supervisor's account and was not tested as a factor in the occurrence.

Findings

From the evidence available, the following findings are made with respect to the collision between a haul truck and a light vehicle on the main ramp of the Stage 4 pit at Bindarra Gold Mine. These findings should not be read as apportioning blame or liability to any particular organisation or individual.

[NOT ESTABLISHED: the application's standard-of-proof sentence, which is inserted by the application]

Contributing factors

  • Mines Safety Guideline MSG-14 did not define a significant change to the road network that would require review of the traffic management plan, and it set no basis for nominating the intersections at which a positive call is required. The plan met the guideline on its face, and the mine was not in breach. This factor existed with virtual certainty. It probably contributed, because a defined trigger and a stated basis would have given a new intersection a route onto the plan's call list, and the guideline made inaction the default. The weight of evidence for this contribution is only just above the standard of proof, because the mine could have held an out-of-cycle review or listed more intersections without any change to the guideline. (Safety Issue)
  • The RL 312 dewatering spur was opened under works order WO-26-4471, which classified the work as routine earthworks and recorded that management of change was not required. This existed with virtual certainty. No referral was made to the traffic management plan owner, the survey department for the in-cab road network or the contractor's technical services group for the collision awareness system geofences, and this very likely contributed to the spur having no stop control or warning sign and to alerts being suppressed at it. Of the 14 new Stage 4 roads cut since the last plan review, the three raised under a management of change record were referred and none of the 11 raised under a works order was. (Safety Issue)
  • The available sight distance at the spur intersection was 41 m against a stopping distance of 96 m for an empty haul truck at the posted speed. This existed with virtual certainty. It very likely contributed because the truck operator could first see the light vehicle's beacon at 53 m and the light vehicle driver could first see the truck at 38 m, which left too little distance for the truck to stop. A hazard report had described the same sight line seven days earlier.
  • The intersection had no stop control, no give-way control, no warning sign, no delineation and no posted speed, although the traffic management plan required a stop control, signalised control or traffic controller where the sight distance rule could not be met. This existed with virtual certainty. It probably contributed, because a stop at the spur mouth would very likely have shown the light vehicle driver the truck, which was within 38 m of view from about 02:47:07.4. The margin from a stop at that distance was thin, and the effect of a sign on the truck rests on the truck operator's own account. (Safety Issue)
  • The traffic management plan required a positive call only at the nine intersections listed at Appendix B, and an intersection could be added only at the annual review. This existed with virtual certainty. It very likely contributed, because the truck had called at each listed intersection it passed that night, the last 51 seconds before the collision, and the RL 312 spur was on neither the Appendix B list nor the road layout drawing. No out-of-cycle review had been held in the plan's eleven year history. (Safety Issue)
  • Neither driver made a positive call before entering the intersection. This existed with virtual certainty, and no call was required at an unlisted intersection. It probably contributed, because a call from either vehicle would have been heard by the other vehicle and by dispatch. A call gives knowledge rather than separation, so the two vehicles would still have had to resolve who went first over 41 m of sight line.
  • The collision awareness system was suppressed at the spur by the S4-LOAD geofence, which was extended up the main ramp on 09/06/2026, and the truck operator and the night shift supervisor did not know the system was off on the ramp. This was very likely the case. It probably contributed through the expectation it created, because a truck operator who believed a quiet system meant an empty ramp had one less reason to expect anyone there. That effect is inferred and could not be measured. An unsuppressed advisory alert would have sounded at about 02:47:06.5, about a second before the brakes were applied, and would have told the operator little that was not already apparent. (Safety Issue)
  • Site access cards were issued without a check that the light vehicle pit driving assessment had been completed. This existed with virtual certainty. The light vehicle driver's card was issued on 09/08/2026 against the contractor's recognition agreement alone, and no pit driving assessment was held for the driver. It probably contributed, because the assessment teaches how to approach an intersection that cannot be seen up. The driver was already giving way to haul trucks as the assessment first requires, and the plan would not have required a call at RL 312, so the contribution is held below that of other factors. (Safety Issue)
  • The light vehicle drove out of the spur onto the ramp without stopping. This existed with virtual certainty. It extremely likely contributed, because without the light vehicle on the ramp there would have been no collision. The driver slowed and looked but did not stop, and the truck was already inside the driver's 38 m of view from the mouth.
  • Neither driver was aware of the other until the truck came over the crest. This was very likely the case, and it very likely contributed, because the collision followed directly from the convergence and nothing in the six seconds that remained could have prevented it.
  • The truck's front left struck the right side of the light vehicle at 24 km/h, pushed it 18.4 m down the ramp and rolled it onto its left side against the inner windrow. This was established with virtual certainty and it contributed with virtual certainty, because the impact and the roll-over produced the injuries: a fractured left clavicle, three fractured left ribs and a small pneumothorax.

Other factors that increased risk

  • The Stage 4 haul roster of 14 consecutive 12 hour 30 minute night shifts existed with virtual certainty, and every limit in the contractor's fatigue management standard was met. It unlikely contributed to this occurrence, because the truck operator's response time of 1.4 seconds was inside the 1.5 seconds the plan allows, and a response time of zero would still have ended in a collision at about 17 km/h instead of 24 km/h. It likely increased risk more generally, because the roster places every haul truck operator at the wheel in the early hours of a tenth, twelfth and fourteenth consecutive night. (Safety Issue)
  • The arrangement under which the night shift extrication capability depends on a second responder called from the accommodation village 11 km from the gatehouse is under examination. The existence of the arrangement is virtually certain. Its influence on this occurrence is recorded at unlikely, because the injuries were complete before the response was paged, and its importance as a risk is recorded at very likely. On the night the extrication, at 03:14, was delayed by approximately 9 minutes waiting for the second responder and the tool. No conclusion has been settled. (Safety Issue)

Other findings

  • The truck operator braked and steered right within 1.4 seconds of the beacon coming into view. This was established with virtual certainty, and it very likely reduced risk. Braking took the impact speed from 37 km/h down to 24 km/h, and the steering turned the truck towards the wall and away from the open pit edge.
  • A wet or slippery ramp surface was very unlikely. The meteorological station recorded no precipitation, the ramp was dry when examined, and the deceleration achieved matched the truck's dry-grade figure. It was considered and not found to contribute.
  • Reduced service brake deceleration was very unlikely. The truck achieved 0.78 m/s2 net, between the 0.80 and 0.82 m/s2 measured in tests either side of the occurrence, and no brake defect had been raised in the preceding twelve months. It was considered and not found to contribute.

Safety issues and actions

This section sets out each safety issue the investigation identified, restates it, and records the safety action taken or proposed against it.

Guideline sets no review trigger and no basis for the positive-call list

Mines Safety Guideline MSG-14 required the traffic management plan to be reviewed after any "significant change" to the road network and required the operator to nominate the intersections at which a positive call was required, but it defined neither the term nor a basis for the nomination.

[NOT ESTABLISHED: any safety action by the State Mines Inspectorate or the guideline's issuer]

Spur opened under a works order, so nothing was referred to anyone

The RL 312 spur was cut under works order WO-26-4471 and classified as routine earthworks, so no management of change record was raised and the traffic management plan owner, the survey department and the contractor's technical services group were not told of the new intersection.

The investigator in charge proposed that ORR-PRO-022 clause 5.3 stop excluding earthworks that create a new intersection with a haul road, or that the works order form at Schedule 4 carry the three referrals held at clause 5.4 of the management of change record: the traffic management plan owner, the survey department for the fleet management system road network, and the contractor's technical services group for the collision awareness system geofences. The proposal noted that of the fourteen new roads cut in Stage 4 since the 12/11/2025 review, the three raised under a management of change record were referred and none of the eleven raised under a works order was. The status is open, with a response due on 30/09/2026.

Access cards issued with no check of the pit driving assessment

The gatehouse issued site access cards against a contractor's recognition agreement alone, without verifying that the Bindarra light vehicle pit driving assessment had been completed, so the light vehicle driver was carded to drive in an operating pit without it.

[NOT ESTABLISHED: any safety action recorded]

[NOT ESTABLISHED: any response from Hallorn Survey & Geotechnical]

Positive calls required only at listed intersections, added only at the annual review

The traffic management plan required a positive call only at the nine intersections listed at Appendix B, and provided no route for adding an intersection between annual reviews, so the RL 312 spur was not a call point.

The Mining Manager, Orrabinda Resources, issued a site-wide direction at 05:10 on 12/08/2026, two hours 23 minutes after the collision. It required a positive call on the pit channel before entering any intersection in the Stage 4 pit, listed in the plan or not, until further notice. The direction was read at the following four pre-starts and posted beside the Appendix B board in the Stage 4 crib room. It remains in force until BIN-TMP-004 is amended.

The investigator in charge proposed that BIN-TMP-004 provide a route by which an intersection reaches Appendix B between annual reviews, and that the plan require a new road to be referred to its owner when it is opened to traffic. The next date on which the RL 312 spur could have been listed was 12/11/2026, three months after the collision. The status is open, with a response due on 30/09/2026.

Collision alerts suppressed at the spur by a geofence operators knew nothing of

The S4-LOAD suppression geofence was extended on 09/06/2026 to a boundary 180 m up-ramp of the RL 312 intersection as a system configuration task, so the collision awareness system raised no alert in the haul truck at the spur, and the operators had not been told.

Tarrowen technical services, as a proactive measure, added suppressed proximity events to the monthly collision awareness report on 28/08/2026, broken down by geofence and by vehicle class, and re-cut the previous twelve months on the same basis for the Stage 4 fleet. The 68 suppressed events inside S4-LOAD, nine of them a light vehicle on the main ramp below the boundary, had been recorded in the system but had not been reported to anyone. The Technical Services Manager, Tarrowen Mining Services, owns the action. It is in progress, with the first report due on 30/09/2026.

The investigator in charge proposed that a change to a suppression geofence boundary be treated as a change to a documented control under ORR-PRO-022 clause 5.2, and that operators be told in writing where the collision awareness system is suppressed and why. The status is open, with a response due on 30/09/2026. The haul truck operator made a similar request at interview, asking that operators be told where the system is turned off.

No stop control or warning sign at an intersection failing the sight distance rule

The RL 312 intersection had a surveyed sight distance of 41 m against a 96 m stopping distance, which did not meet clause 6.2 of the traffic management plan, and it had no stop control, warning sign or delineation.

The Mining Manager, Orrabinda Resources, barricaded the RL 312 spur and closed it to all traffic on the night of the occurrence, and it remained closed. On 14/08/2026, before the November reissue of Schedule 1, survey measured the available sight distance at the other ten unlisted roads cut in Stage 4 since the last review. Two of the ten were below the clause 6.2 minimum and were closed pending a stop control. The action is closed for the RL 312 spur, and the two further roads remain open as actions. The haul truck operator also asked at interview that a sign be put on the intersection and the road be shown on the in-cab map.

[NOT ESTABLISHED: any action on the locations of the three other hazard reports, from 03/2025, 09/2025 and 02/2026, that each described a light vehicle and a haul truck meeting unexpectedly at an unlisted intersection]

Haul operators rostered for fourteen consecutive 12.5 hour night shifts

The contractor's Stage 4 haul roster of 14 nights on and 7 off, within its fatigue management standard, placed haul truck operators at the wheel in the early hours of consecutive night shifts, although the evidence did not show that it contributed to this collision.

[NOT ESTABLISHED: any action recorded against the roster]

Night shift extrication waits on a second responder called from the village

The night shift was rostered with one qualified mines rescue paramedic on site, and the second responder, who had to be present before an extrication began, was called in from the accommodation village 11 km away with the hydraulic rescue tool. The matter is still being examined.

[NOT ESTABLISHED: any action recorded]

Control of light vehicle entry to operating pits

The night shift supervisor said there was no permit, radio call-in, board or check by which the supervisor of an operating pit knew which light vehicles were in it, and asked for one of these to be introduced.

[NOT ESTABLISHED: any action on a light vehicle entry control for operating pits]

- [The occurrence] - Timeline entry "The light vehicle leaves the bore collar": both endpoints are recorded as approximate ("about 02:45 to about 02:47"), yet a duration of 2 m 06 s is given. This precision is not supported by estimated endpoints. The scaffold's "about 02:45" departure is also a reconstruction, since the driver's own estimate (about ten to three) postdates the collision. - First sighting distance: the truck operator estimated about forty metres (interview and ASR-2026-0341). The survey and FMS give 53 m. The draft presents both. - Light vehicle speed (about 25 km/h) and not stopping at the spur mouth come only from the light vehicle driver's interview, which is not finalised. - The causal chain "Truck operator braked and steered right within 1.4 seconds of the beacon appearing -> critical event" links a mitigating action directly to the injury outcome. Its category is not stated. - The factor "Haul truck operator fatigued during the approach to the intersection" is tagged on the 02:47:06 timeline entry but has no category or test result given. - The scaffold line for 06/08 states "Nobody outside the dewatering department was told about it." The source states only that the report was not referred to four named parties. - [Context] - Night shift supervisor interview notes: asked whether he knew the collision awareness system was suppressed at RL 312, the answer is recorded as "Yes". The same notes say he did not know the geofence had been extended to the ramp, and the geofence factor states he said he did not know the system was off on the ramp. The "Yes" appears to mean he knew after the collision. The note should be clarified. - Occurrence notification ORR-OCC-2026-0332 states as fact that the operator saw the beacon "about 53 m above the spur". The dust factor's influence note says this sighting point is inferred from the last steady data point and the survey, not recorded. The operator himself estimated about forty metres. - Emergency response log summary gives "First response vehicle on scene in 7 minutes". This is 7 minutes from the collision (02:47 to 02:54) but 6 minutes from the page at 02:48. The reference point should be stated. - [Safety analysis / Organisational Influences] - Access cards issued with no check of the pit driving assessment: the evidence attributes the open question on the site supplement to Hallorn's own records, while the investigator notes place it with the training coordinator. The two sources should be reconciled. - Access cards issued with no check of the pit driving assessment: the driver's statements (never having heard of the assessment, never having seen BIN-TMP-004, and that he would have called if told to) appear only in the factor's evidence text.
